msItem.incipit: Death rode a-hunting once to kill a doe Folger First Line Index

abstract.p: The poem imagines Death as a huntsman who becomes so taken with a black horse—both for its colour and its smooth ambling pace—that he never dismounts, turning a conventional emblem of death into a comic figure with personal taste. The choice of an ambling horse carries a further nuance: its steady, effortless motion suggests the continuous and unhurried progress of death itself, not sudden violence but an ever-present advance. At the same time, amblers were associated with comfort and status, giving Death an almost gentlemanly preference that heightens the humour. The closing advice to Jacke Potter exploits this conceit by mock-practicality suggesting that he avoid such horses and choose a rougher trotter instead, as if one might evade Death simply by changing one’s mount.

lg.l: Death rodd a hunting once to kill a doe
On a blacke nagg; whose pace did please him so,
And colour to (for death delights in blacke)
That never since hee would gett of his backe:
If death love ambling naggs; Prithee Jacke Pootter
Buy no more ambler, but goe begg a Trotter.
